questions.prompt: A foundry has its best profit year, but quality judgment still lives mostly in the founder's eye and apprentices only see final inspection stamps. What should the new president do before commissioning a plaque?
choices: Turn rejected-casting review into a repeat apprentice ritual
Celebrate first because profit proves the system is durable
Keep quality judgment informal so apprentices respect the founder
questions.explanation: The ritual transfers judgment into institutional practice. A plaque or informal mystique leaves the capability dependent on one person.

questions.prompt: A newsroom wins an award for an investigation, but the source-check method from that work is not used in new projects and the next kickoff is already scheduled. What is the durability risk?
choices: The newsroom may be too modest about public recognition
The award becomes a story instead of a protocol that shapes future work
The team will never be allowed to celebrate
questions.explanation: Durability requires the method to become routine. The issue is not celebration; it is whether recognition replaces the discipline that earned it.

questions.prompt: A credit union doubles its branches and wants training to focus on growth pride. Three declined loans show the lending discipline that protected members. What should training include?
choices: Reviews of declined loans that teach the member-protection standard
Only merger wins so new managers feel confident
A sales contest to prove the merger has energy
questions.explanation: The declined loans carry the discipline into scale. Growth pride and sales energy can dilute the judgment that created member trust.

questions.prompt: A research institute receives a major grant. Senior scientists want to approve spending before any challenge to the flagship hypothesis. What is the durable move?
choices: Assign a junior scientist to challenge the hypothesis before spending is approved
Delay debate so funders see quick action
Treat the grant as proof that the hypothesis no longer needs pressure
questions.explanation: The challenge protects the disciplined thought that made the institute worth funding. Quick spending and proof language let success silence debate.

questions.prompt: A botanical garden's new conservatory draws crowds, while seed-bank freezer maintenance is easy to postpone. What question should govern the board packet?
choices: Which photo will impress visitors most?
Which operating rhythm gives the institution lasting value after attention fades?
How can the seed bank be hidden until donations slow?
questions.explanation: Durability asks what practice must survive popularity. Impressive photos and hiding quiet work both let attention outrank institutional value.

questions.prompt: A foundation beats its campaign goal and wants a gala montage. Donor stewardship reviews are not ready. What should happen next?
choices: Run the montage because record donations should be celebrated immediately
Stop all celebration permanently
Prepare the first-year impact review before making the campaign a victory-lap event
questions.explanation: The impact review turns success into stewardship. The issue is not whether people may celebrate, but whether donors receive disciplined follow-through.

questions.prompt: A leader says, "We made the leap, so the disciplines are now part of who we are." What warning should you bring back?
choices: Identity can replace practice unless routines, reviews, and boundaries keep the disciplines alive
Success should be distrusted because it always ruins organizations
The only safe response to success is to avoid new goals
questions.explanation: The warning targets complacency, not success itself. Durable greatness needs practiced standards after the leap, not slogans about identity.

questions.prompt: A routine created during the turnaround still exists, but no decision changes when the routine surfaces new evidence. What should leaders conclude?
choices: The routine is durable because it still appears on the calendar
The routine may have become ceremony and needs renewal or removal
All routines are dangerous after success
questions.explanation: Durability is not empty preservation. A routine must keep shaping decisions; otherwise discipline has turned into paperwork with history.

questions.prompt: You can ask one closing question after a major win. Which question best converts achievement into repeated operating habit?
choices: Who should tell the story of this win most often?
How quickly can we move on so nobody gets complacent?
Which routine, review, or boundary must still exist six months from now for this win to keep earning itself?
questions.explanation: The question turns the win into a practice test. Storytelling alone can become display, and moving on too fast may skip the transfer of discipline.

reviewCards.front: A win is being turned into a plaque. What durability question should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Ask what routine, review, or boundary will carry the discipline forward after the celebration fades.

reviewCards.front: An award recognizes great work, but the method is not being reused. What is at risk?
reviewCards.back: The award may become self-image instead of institutional practice. Convert the method into the next kickoff, training, or review.

reviewCards.front: Success makes debate feel less necessary. Which discipline should come back?
reviewCards.back: Disciplined thought. Keep challenge routines alive especially after funding, praise, or growth makes the answer feel proven.

reviewCards.front: A quiet practice competes with a popular new success. What should decide funding?
reviewCards.back: Fund the practice that gives lasting institutional value, not merely the visible object receiving attention.

reviewCards.front: A legacy routine still exists but no longer changes choices. What should you do?
reviewCards.back: Renew or remove it. Durability means living discipline, not ceremonial preservation.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is converting a win into durable practice. You identify the discipline that created the result, then embed it in a routine, review, training, or boundary that survives attention and comfort.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a team celebrates a win, then name the practice that earned it before choosing the symbol that celebrates it.
If success adds scale, then train new people on the noes and standards that protected the original trust.
If outside validation arrives, then run the same debate or fact-check routine before approving the next spend.
If a routine no longer changes decisions, then renew its decision link or stop pretending it is discipline.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, choose one recent win and write the routine, review, or boundary that must still exist six months from now.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, take one celebration, award, or growth milestone and convert one part of it into training, a checklist, or a review rhythm.

memorableLines.text: The win is safest before it becomes a story about itself.
memorableLines.why: It warns against victory-lap thinking without attacking celebration.

memorableLines.text: A win becomes durable when it teaches the institution how to keep earning it.
memorableLines.why: It captures the closing move in one practical sentence.

memorableLines.text: The plaque can wait until the practice can stand without it.
memorableLines.why: It gives the reader a concrete image for choosing practice before display.
